speechtext: FITZPATRICK (Minister of Justice) moved first reading of Bill (No. 147) to amend the Acts relating to Naturalization of Aliens. He said : This Bill will apply exclusively to the province of Quebec, and is designed to meet a difficulty which exists there. In that province applications tor naturalization must be made to a judge cf the circuit court of the district in which the alien resides. But the circuit court of a district travels from place to place, and the question has arisen whether or not the applications must be made to the courtsitting in the chief place of the county. It is a trifling matter, and I cannot understand how the difficulty has arisen, but probably some clerk of the court wants to avoid difficulty, and I am asked to make the point clear.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

The management of the Maynooth post office under the late postmaster was extremely unsatisfactory owing to continuous carelessness in the handling of mail matter and in the general management of the office. Not only was this the case in
respect of unregistered but also of registered letters, serious delays occurring in their delivery. Numerous complaints because of such irregularities were made on behalf of patrons, but nevertheless the irregularities instead of being remedied were allowed to continue without any abatement. The postmaster himself gave little or no attention to the office leaving its management to the clerks, who were constantly changing, and who continued to make mistakes, frequently delivering mail matter to the wrong persons and making other mistakes. An official investigation was held which showed the management to be as above mentioned and in consequence a change was made in the postmastership, Mr. James Haryett being appointed postmaster.

I have no desire to prolong the session more than is necessary, but I must enter my protest against the commencement of morning sittings at this time. Possibly, the right hon. First Minister has not taken into consideration the important committee work that is yet to be done. We have important questions before the Railway Committee, and the Committee on Banking and Commerce, and there is at least one special committee, of which I have the honour of being a mem-iter, a committee which is sitting. I might almost say, day by day and endeavouring to get into shape the very important Bill respecting the inspection of grain. The committee has not yet finished with that Bill, and we shall require to have, at any rate, one more sitting if not more. Before the Orders of the Day are called. Mr. Speaker. I rise to make a personal explanation. I find the following in this morning's ' Citizen ' on the first editorial page :
Of what does Hon. Sydney Fisher's military experience consist ? Has he ever taken a rifle to defend his country ? No, this does not suit his book. What he prefers is that some one else should do the fighting and he should draw the pay. Mr. Rufus Pope, M.P., made a statement recently in the House of Commons to the effect that the Hon. Sydney Fisher, M.P., for Brome and Minister of Agriculture in the government of Canada, once lent a horse to a trooper in a cavalry corps who was entitled to and received from government the sum of $12 for the horse during the twelve days of camp. Was Mr. Fisher satisfied with this horse-hire? It was the amount allowed by this government of which he was then a member to enable a trooper to provide himdelf with a horse and was thus fixed as a fai-r equivalent. No, this did not suit our modern Shylock. ' The responsible minister for the district,' demands from the trooper not only the amount allowed for the services of the horse but in addition the poor fellow's hard-earned and paltry pittance of fifty cents a day !
Having looked up ' Hansard.' I find that the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope) did make some such statement in the House ns is here referred to. I was not paying any attention to the hon. gentleman. aDd therefore did not deny his statement at the time. I have only this to say : It is true

that, a few years ago, I was keeping a horse in a livery stable in Ottawa. It was the duty of the livery stable keeper to exercise the horse when I was away. On one occasion, during my absence, the livery stable keeper let the horse to a trooper of the Princess Louise Dragoon Guards. No charge was made for the use of the horse ; I did not receive any money for the use of the horse either from the trooper who used it or from anybody else. The statements made in this editorial are absolutely false and have no foundation in fact. I find that some hon. gentleman think that what the hon. member for Compton said was in regard to a horse in the eastern townships. I have only to say that I never let a horse to anybody or received any pay for any horse, either in the eastern townships or here or anvwhere else, that was to be used in the militia of Canada.

He returned to his duties within a week, and the railway company was astute enough to get a settlement with him. When he returned he thought he was quite well. Tlhey paid him $400. But a short time afterwards he found that his spine was affected, and he suffered great pain and was incapacitated for work of all kinds.
Are we to understand that his salary was going on, at the same time and that "he received mileage as well ?

I am not complaining about that. There was an accident somewhere along the line near the city of Guelph a year or two ago where some other men in the employ of the Post Office Department were injured. May I ask if these men were paid their salary and mileage as well ?

The case of Mr. Cheney is perhaps the one my hon. friend has in mind. Mr. Cheney was injured and the Grand Trunk Railway Company compensated him for his losses, the controller thinks, to the amount of $1,700. The department transferred him to the inside service at London at an increased rate of salary so as to make up the increase of salary which he was losing by the loss of mileage.

May I ask the hon. gentleman if there are not cases other than that of Mr. Sloan not provided for by the department ?
Sir WILLIAM MULOCIv. The officers are not aware of any other case. It is a rule I inaugurated when I came into office to take into account injuries to or deaths occasioned by railway accidents of. railway mail clerks. If my hon. friend is aware of any case that is entitled to consideration I would be very grateful to him if he would bring it to the attention of the department.

I would like to ask the hon. Postmaster General as a matter of im-Mr. CLANCY.
formation if any provision is made in his department for paying some portion if not the whole of a reasonable life insurance for employees who are occupying hazardous positions such as those of mail clerks and who are liable to lose their lives or be injured ?
I do not think there has been any provision in the law of the character to which my hon. friend alludes.

I would like to call the hon. gentleman's attention to what seems to be a very common practice in the departments ; that is paying for life insurance policies for men who go out of this city on government business. If there is any justification for this practice-I do not say whether there is or not-it seems to me that those persons like railway mail clerks who are forced in to hazardous positions should be considered and that it would be only a just thing to contribute a portion if not the whole of the premiums on insurance policies upon the lives of these persons so engaged. I cannot imagine that I could have anything but the approval of the hon. gentleman for the course which I propose in view of what seems to be a very common practice of the departments of paying the premiums upon the insurance policies of persons who are temporarily travelling on government business. I would like to know if the hon. gentleman is prepared to consider that matter?

The policy that the Post Office Department has adopted seems to me to.be better than the one which my hon. friend suggests. Whenever a railway mail clerk is killed it is our policy to vote the sum of $2,000 as a gratuity to his dependents, so that practically we are not only paying the premium but we are undertaking that the amount is paid in case an accident happens.
In case of disablement ?

There is always a compassionate consideration for disablement. My hon. friend does not know anything about the working of the department. He cannot point to a single case since I have been in charge of the department where there has been no consideration given to a railway mail clerk who has met with an accident. I think we are doing very well for the clerks in living up to this policy. There is nothing in the law about it, but I trust it will be always adhered to. I am told there is a practise in some of the departments like this : A civil servant who has occasion to travel on a railway and who travels free, as a good many employees of the government are allowed to do, has no cause of action against the railway company in ease of accident; therefore in such

a ease the employee Is allowed to take out an accident policy and to charge tihe premium in his travelling expenses. That, I am told by my deputy, is the extent to which the departments recognize responsibility tor acidents occurring to employees. If, of course, a man were paying his way and had a cause of action against the railway company in case of accident it might be different.

Has there been any test case in regard to employees of the government travelling on the railway establishing the fact that in the event of injury they are without redress under the law, though the accident may have been due to the culpable negligence of some of the railway employees ?

I do not know whether it has been determined as a matter of law but I think the companies, in connection with any free transportation, add the stipulation that a person travelling under these conditions shall have no recourse against the company, he giving no consideration fer the service rendered by the railway company. It is treated as a matter of courtesy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That stipulation is on our own passes.
I admit that but I do not think that many of us believe that it could be sustained in a court of law.
We cannot give a free opinion on that point.

I understand the hon. Postmaster General to say that this was the practice of the railway companies and I supposed it had been tested by some decision of a court that would give strength to it. But I have heard that contention disputed over and over again by legal authorities who have claimed that it was not optional for any company to put any provision' on a pass or on a shipping Bill of that kind and to say that provided you accept so and so you accept it on conditions. Insurance companies do the same thing but when you go into a court of law the court determines whether the conditions are proper and reasonable and if they are unreasonable the court will not hold you as bound by these conditions notwithstanding that you sent your goods under the conditions of that Shipping Bill or tha-t you accepted a pass on those terms.
Mr. BLA1N. I understand that the Postmasters give no bonds to the government or rather that the government guarantee the fulfilment of the duties of the postmasters. I understand that the postmasters pay into a fund! and that when there is a loss sustained by any postmaster it is repaid out
of tfne fund which is accumulated by the government.

The practice in the department now is to assess the employees instead of having guarantee bonds for their fidelity, but it is not enforced in the case of postmasters at offices having a revenue of less than $100. The rate charged is 40 cents for each $100 of insurance. That is the rate which I understand prevails throughout Canada. The fund is deposited in the savings bank account to the credit of the guarantee fund. If a loss occurs it is then chargeable against it and an applica tion is made to the government for an Order in Council allowing the withdrawal of the fund. We have been very fortunate so far although running many risks. We recently had a loss of $10,000 which occurred through the misconduct or robbery of a mail clerk in the west. Part of that money has been recovered. That would have made a bad hole in our fund but we have not been called upon to make it good. I suppose we will have to make some of it good. Altogether it is a more satisfactory system than having a bond for each officer. In the latter case there is the danger of the bond expiring, and there is trouble in seeing to the renewal of it, and the payment of premiums. and in the event of loss we are not always able to recover, although there is no moral deubt as to the liability of the company. For instance, some time ago $367 disappeared, and there was no doubt that it disappeared by the fault of one of three of our officers, but which one it was impossible to state. In that case we could not tell which officer was responsible and we could not have recovered from the insurance company. The three men were insured under our own system and we were able to make good the loss. There are many advantages in the system ; having tried it for seven years I think it is infinitely better than the old system.
What was the old system ?

Each postmaster gave an insurance company bond or a private bond. In the latter case, all sorts of obstacles were put in the way of recovering. The minister was told that it would be a great hardship to seek to recover against some bondsman who had not the money. It was a perfect nuisance, and I think my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) who has had experience will agree with me in that. I must say that defaults in the postal service are not frequent, and that on the whole we have a most efficient and honest staff throughout the country, but unfortunately occasionally some one will lapse.
I do not complain of the new system. Could the minister state how much was paid into the fund last year and how much was paid out of it.

If my hou. friend wishes I will bring that down on the supplementary estimates. It is a special trust fund and the premiums do not go into the consolidated revenue at all. By an Act passed in 1898 the money assessed upon the officers is treated as independently as if it were a private insurance company.
Do I understand that instead. of these officers paying to a guarantee company, they pay so much to the government and the government guarantees ?
That is practically it; we do our own insuring. We take the premiums and put them in this trust fund, out of which any loss is paid.
How has it worked, out ?

Satisfactorily. If the few years' experience we have had furnishes reliable data for all time, then it would be most satisfactory. However, there might be a serious loss any day, and I do not think we should debate the extent to which money passes through the post office.
Does each official get a guarantee bond in the regular way ?

Instead of an official giving a guarantee bond or getting neighbours to act as his bondsmen, in a case where an employee would be bonded for say $500, he pays a premium to this fund of 40 cents on the dollar or $2 a year. That is deducted from his salary and goes to the trust fund.
It seems to be cheaper than the other system.
I would suggest to the Postmaster General that this would be interesting information to put in his annual report. How does that matter of'the loss df $10,000 in the Northwest now stand ?

Nothing has been adjusted yet. The total amount stolen was $10,000, and we have recovered nearly $7,000.	'

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We make an estimate every year on the amount of annuities that will be necessary. Of course, it is impossible to make an exact estimate because we cannot know exactly how many Indians will be alive and entitled to these annuities. We think we are safe with this reduced estimate. Also in making calculations for this year we must take into account moneys placed at the credit of the Indian Fund as a result of the settlement of accounts between the old province of Canada and the Dominion, and this tends to reduce the vote.

In what state are the surveys that were commenced some time ago on Walpole Island ? I understood that they had commenced but it is reported to me that they had been stopped or delayed for some reason, but I do not know just what the reason was.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that instructions have been given to have this survey made. But it has not been possible to get it done. It is extremely difficult to get survey work done at present, because the enormous amount of surveying that we are doing in the west takes up practically all the available men.
Is there any objection on the part of the Indians, or any of them, to the survey being made ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Some objections were made, but after considering them we decided to go on, nevertheless.
Did the department decide [DOT] to go on, notwithstanding the objection of the Indians, as a matter of policy, or did the Indians finally consent ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a matter of which I have no personal knowledge. I think the objections were made in connection with the holdings of the Indians.
You are carrying on surveys on the islands in the Georgian bay. Are there not a number of islands there under the Indian Department ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We had surveys made some years ago, I am qot aware that any have been made since then. There are some islands that are now in dispute between the Ontario government and the Dominion government, and it is only when the consent of the Ontario government has first been secured that we make any sales. The sales are of an unimportant character, the islands are small and of no great value.

Has the minister considered that difficulty will arise in a place like Walpole Island where improvements were made without any regard to surveys? How does he propose working out the question of the settlement of holdings ? Or has he a system of making, of uniform size the lots Indians may hold ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The policy is to survey the land where it is actually occupied by the Indians, that is the purpose in view.

I have some acquaintance with the condition of things there where the lands are held by the Indians. I think when the hon. gentleman surVeys the holdings of what the Indians claim to occupy now, he will have some strangely shaped lots left that are not claimed by the Indians, unless he has some system.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a question either of surveying the lots as they are or of not surveying them at all, and leaving the boundaries altogether undefined. It is a delicate question, and all we can do is to act on the best information we can obtain, and survey the lots according to actual location. I have not myself personal knowledge of the particular matter to which the hon. gentleman has called my attention.

I have not understood that the Indians made any demand. I may say that the gentleman who is employed by the government, Mr. McGeorge, is as good a man as can be found. I have understood,
I do not know whether the information is accurate, that the Indians were somewhat opposed to this, and made no demand for a subdivision survey.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot give a positive answer whether any demands from the Indians came, but I will give my hon. friend a full statement with regard to the whole matter.
What method does the department adopt In the sale of timber on the islands belonging to the Indians in Georgian bay, or elsewhere ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No timber is sold by the Indian Department except under the regulations providing for the sale of timber generally. Applications have been made for sale of timber on these islands, but 1 have refused to sell.
I understood you sold tome timber not very long ago on the Georgian bay, not very far from Midland.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In one case, some years ago. I found, some time after it had been done, that the officials of the department had sold some land on Batchewana bay which had some hardwood on it. They sold the laud including the wood. The persons to whom it was sold had made applications for the land, the land was sold in the regular way and no reservation of the timioer was 'made. The timber was not of any special value, 4out if the matter had been brought to my attention I would have directed that the timber be sold separately, In accordance with the regulations. I do not imagine that this is the case to which my hoii. friend refers. With that one exception, there has been absolutely no sale of timber lands, except in accordance with the regulations.
How long is it since the regulation was made requiring that Indian lands must be sold by public auction ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The regulation was made before I came*into office, and there has Teen no change.
We had a discussion here only a few nights ago in regard to this very question, when it was stated that Indian lands had been sold without competition to a party living in Orillia.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Those were not Indian lands.
This department has no authority to sell any other land there. It either belongs to the Indians and is controlled here, or belongs to the province of Ontario and is controlled at Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What the House was discussing the other night was not sold by the Indian Department.
What department sold it, then ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I presume it was sold by the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
That department may have had the land for the purposes of the department, and then sold it.
That may be.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All Indian land is required by Order in Council, passed some years ago, to be sold by public competition, and, as I say, with that one exception, there has been none solid without reference to that regulation.
I think the hon. minister is perhaps right, because I understood that this land was transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
